source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug and Alcohol Dependence 131 (2013) 23-35, all 13 pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; pp. 23-33 rendered at 150 dpi to check every number, with Tables 4 and 5 (pp. 27-32) also at 300 dpi.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the review's evidence; the claim is more cautious than the review's abstract and says why. Two details in the statement are not reproduced as worded, and a few are imprecise. (1) 'Eight other European countries' should be seven: the eight-country study (Gilchrist et al., 2011) covered Greece, Spain, Bulgaria, Italy, Slovenia, Slovakia, Poland and Scotland, and Scotland is part of the UK (Table 4, p. 28). (2) 'At least six study summaries ... moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive' (editors' count): I count five that say so of attitudes overall: Giannetti (moderate), Happell and Taylor (neutral), an unnamed row that is Kelleher and Cotter (appropriate, positive), Pinikahana (positive) and Saitz (positive). A sixth needs a borderline case: Foster and Onyeukwu, whose summary calls attitudes suboptimal with only permissiveness moderate, or Strauser, whose stigma was 'below the criteria for negative stigma'. Suggest 'at least five'. (3) The response-rate range '31% to 92% where given' omits Strauser et al. ('all participated', 100%) and Segal and Dittrich (3.9% refusal); 31-92% is the range of printed percentages only. (4) 'The one included study that observed care': the review counts two studies using observation (p. 26); Segal and Dittrich is the only one that rated the quality of care from observation, while Curtis and Harrison used participant observation in a qualitative study. (5) In the magnitude, '5 papers link more experience or contact with more positive attitudes': the review says 'more positive or different attitudes' (p. 29), and one of the five (Russell et al.) concerns disease-model beliefs. (6) 'Training ... went with more positive attitudes' should note that education went with worse attitudes where role support was low (Ford et al., 2008; pp. 30, 32).
claims.note: Checked on the rendered pages (pp. 23-33, Tables 4-5 at 300 dpi). Matches: 2000 to 2011 (January 2000 to November 2011, English or Dutch, PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase); 28 studies; 12 Australia, 7 UK, 5 USA, 1 Canada, 1 Ireland, 1 eight-country European, 1 USA-UK (sum 28); 20 quantitative, 5 interview or focus-group, 2 implicit association test, 2 observation (these overlap: sum 29); 866 professionals; 92 clients in Sydney residential rehabilitation; 2,864 HIV patients, 17.1% currently injecting, 373 physicians, 23.2%; 683 observations, nine services, California, 1985-1986, better care on all 4 criteria. 'At most 25 independent samples' is right as an upper bound: Table 4 marks Brener 2007/2010a and Ford 2008/2009/2011 as shared samples (28 - 3 = 25). Happell et al. (2002) and Pinikahana et al. (2002) also look like overlapping samples that the review does not mark: both are crisis assessment and treatment teams in metropolitan Melbourne and rural Victoria with 134 registered nurses, so 24 is likely. The attribution of the treatment-completion finding to Brener et al. (2010a) in the text (p. 32) is confirmed wrong: Table 4 and Table 5 and the reference list show it is Brener et al. (2010b). That Segal and Dittrich appears only in Tables 4-5 and the references, never in the text, is confirmed. The abstract's consequence statements correspond in the Discussion (p. 33) to Curtis and Harrison (empowerment and treatment outcomes) and Peckover and Chidlaw (shorter, task-oriented visits), both qualitative. Not mentioned by the claim: the review's text (p. 32) also reports that patients judged their professionals more favourably when the professionals' attitudes were more positive (Brener et al., 2007), whereas Table 5 (p. 30) gives that study's client finding as clients at services with more HCV-positive people rating their professionals more favourably; the text and table disagree. Other internal inconsistencies: Gilchrist's setting breakdown (92 + 80 + 81 = 253) does not add up to 866 (Table 4); Gilchrist's Table 5 summary says there were no differences by professional group, yet names the highest-regard professions and physicians outside addiction services as lowest; the study-population categories in 3.2 sum to 27, not 28; one Table 5 row has no study name (p. 31). The 1985-1986 data in Segal and Dittrich fall outside the review's 2000-2011 window, which is a publication-date window (published 2001).

anchors.extracted: Three databases searched for 2000-2011; 1562 citations; 28 studies included. Abstract states professionals generally had negative attitudes; that negative attitudes diminished patients' empowerment and later treatment outcomes; and that professionals were less involved and more task-oriented. Concludes negative attitudes are common and contribute to suboptimal care, while noting that few studies evaluated consequences.

anchors.locator: Methods, 2.1 Search strategy; 2.2 Study selection, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: PubMed, PsycINFO and Embase searched for articles in English or Dutch published January 2000 to November 2011. Titles screened by one reviewer, with a random 10% double-screened (94% agreement); abstracts and full texts judged by two independent reviewers.

anchors.locator: Fig. 1; Methods, 2.2 Study selection (continued) and 2.3 Data extraction
anchors.extracted: 1575 records (PubMed 1170, PsycINFO 10, Embase 395), 13 duplicates, 1562 titles, 420 abstracts, 55 full texts, 28 included. Excluded at the abstract stage included 34 on education/training or students; at full text, 4 on education/training of professionals and 10 Asian, African or South American studies (excluded as culturally different). Studies quality-rated with Buckley et al. indicators. Data extracted by one author and verified by a second; results synthesised thematically because of heterogeneity, with no quantitative pooling.
All 28 met the quality threshold (at least 7 of 11 Buckley indicators, one of which asks whether the response rate is acceptable), so equal weight was given to every study.

12 studies from Australia, 7 UK, 5 USA, 1 Canada, 1 Ireland, 1 cross-country comparison of eight European countries, 1 USA-UK comparison. 20 quantitative (SAAS used in 5, AAPPQ in 4), 5 interview or focus-group studies, 2 implicit association tests, 2 using observation (categories overlap).

anchors.locator: Results, 3.3 Attitudes of health professionals, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 29)
anchors.extracted: Professionals generally negative. Eight-country European study: regard for working with substance users, especially drug users, consistently lower than for patients with depression or diabetes (Gilchrist et al., 2011). Focus groups of 35 professionals preferred that specialists provide care. Nurses poorly motivated and dissatisfied (Ford et al., 2008). Vignette study: more stigmatizing attitudes to active substance use disorder than to other mental illnesses, more positive to people recovering, abstaining and working (Rao et al., 2009).

Some studies found positive attitudes (Pinikahana et al., 2002, mental-health professionals; Saitz et al., 2002, primary care physicians). Physicians outside specialised addiction services reported the lowest regard and addiction-service staff higher regard (Gilchrist); forensic psychiatric nurses and anaesthesiologists more negative than comparison professionals. Five studies: more personal or work experience or contact went with 'more positive or different' attitudes.

Gilchrist et al. (2011): 866 professionals in GR, ES, BG, IT, SI, SK, PL and Scotland, 73% response (setting breakdown 92 + 80 + 81). Brener et al. (2010b): Sydney residential rehabilitation, 92 clients, mixed methods. Ding et al. (2005): 2,864 HIV patients, 17.1% currently injecting, 373 physicians (75% response). Segal and Dittrich (2001): 683 observations in 9 psychiatric emergency services in California, visits 1985-1986, 3.9% refusal. Printed response rates 31% (May) to 92% (Saitz); Strauser 'all participated'; Russell unknown. Same-sample marks: Brener 2007/2010a; Ford 2008/2009/2011.

Gilchrist: regard lowest for drug and alcohol problems, lowest among physicians outside specialised addiction services. Summaries describing attitudes as moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive: Giannetti (moderate), Happell and Taylor (neutral), unnamed emergency-department row (appropriate; positive), Pinikahana (positive), Saitz (positive); borderline: Foster and Onyeukwu (suboptimal, permissiveness moderate), Strauser (below the criterion for negative stigma). Brener 2010b: perceived staff discrimination predicted treatment drop-out. Ding: 23.2% of patients had physicians with negative attitudes to people who inject drugs; attitudes not associated with patients' reported problems with care, satisfaction, unmet needs or access. Segal and Dittrich: substance-use cases received better quality of care on all 4 criteria, though attitudes were not always positive.

anchors.locator: Results, 3.4 Explanations for negative attitudes, 2nd-4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Perceived controllability linked to negative attitudes (Brener 2010a; Strauser). Low knowledge reported widely; some studies found training and education went with more positive attitudes (Ding, Happell and Taylor, Howard and Holmshaw, May), but education was counterproductive where role support from colleagues was low (Ford 2008); organisational and role support linked to therapeutic commitment.

anchors.locator: Results, 3.5 Consequences of attitudes on healthcare delivery, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 33)
anchors.extracted: Only a few studies examined consequences for care. Patients reporting more perceived discrimination by professionals and dissatisfaction were less likely to complete treatment (cited to Brener 2010a; the study is 2010b). Patients judged professionals more favourably when professionals' attitudes were more positive (Brener 2007). Ding et al. found no association between physicians' negative attitudes and patients' reports of problems, dissatisfaction or access. Segal and Dittrich is not mentioned.

Effects on empowerment and treatment outcomes rest on Curtis and Harrison (2001), a qualitative study, which suggests clinicians may impose beliefs and impede collaboration; shorter visits, visits in pairs and a task-oriented approach rest on Peckover and Chidlaw (2007), interviews with 18 district nurses.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 4.1 Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph; 4.2 Conclusion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Limitations: possible missed studies; articles without abstract or full text excluded; English and Dutch only; primary studies affected by selection of motivated participants and by self-report and social desirability. Conclusion: most studies found negative attitudes; more studies of consequences, ideally longitudinal, are needed.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed; location addition only: 'lowest among physicians outside addiction services' is at p. 29 (3.3, 3rd paragraph) and Table 5 (p. 31), not on p. 26 or in Table 4 as the locator implies.

Confirmed as written. The card's sixth summary is Strauser et al. ('below the criterion for negative stigma'), which is not one of the four words; the claim and the card's interpretation-gap text compress this to 'six ... moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive' (see missed).

reporting_issues.note: PsycINFO's 10 records are confirmed (Fig. 1, p. 25), but the set logic is misdescribed (Table 1, p. 26). Sets #31 and #32 require a substance-use term plus the 'attitude of health personnel' term plus a care-delivery (#31) or stigma (#32) term. Set #30 needs no attitude term: it requires a health-personnel term, a substance-use term, and both a care-delivery and a stigma term. Correct statement: every retrieved record needed a care-delivery or stigma term (set #30 needed both), so attitude studies indexed without either were not retrieved. The consequence stated on the card stands.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from the unmet critical items 2, 4, 7 and 13, each borne out by the article. Item 9 at partial yes is generous but defensible: the Buckley checklist has confounding and subject-appropriateness items, yet every study passed and no per-study ratings are given. Item 1 at 'no' follows the project's convention for reviews without a comparator. Neither changes the overall judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right: the abstract's causal statements on consequences rest on two qualitative studies, and the review's text omits the one observational study with the opposite result. One wording fix in results_show: 'at least six papers' summaries ... moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive' should say five, plus one (Strauser et al.) with stigma below the criterion for negative stigma, matching the card's own KF 6.

missed: The '8 European countries' in Gilchrist et al. (2011) include Scotland (Table 4, p. 28: GR, ES, BG, IT, SI, SK, PL and Scotland). The card does not note this, and the claim derived from it says 'eight other European countries' alongside the UK; the countries outside the UK and Ireland are seven.

Minor: the design counts in 3.2 (20 quantitative, 5 interview or focus-group, 2 implicit association test, 2 observation) sum to 29 for 28 papers, so the categories overlap (for example, the implicit-association-test studies are also quantitative); KF 3 repeats them as if exclusive.

Minor: the two 'observation' studies are Segal and Dittrich (observed quality of care) and Curtis and Harrison (participant observation within a qualitative study). Only the first measured care delivered, which is how RI 1 rightly describes it.
